  The save is scattered: browser downloads land in Downloads (Chrome on
  Android saves every download to the shared Downloads folder by default,
  Internal Storage/Download — verified this run from three guides that agree
  on the path), Gallery-made GIFs land in the gallery's GIFs album (Samsung
  Gallery Create GIF, Google Photos Create GIF — verified this run from two
  video walkthroughs), app-saved GIFs land in Pictures or Downloads. And the
  chat apps that show GIFs do not keep .gif files at all — WhatsApp converts
  a sent GIF into a short looping MP4 video behind the scenes (verified this
  run: ezyimg, wildandfreetools, convertico all agree, conversion automatic
  and cannot be opted out of), Telegram treats GIFs as silent MPEG-4 video
  and its Save to GIFs writes nothing to the phone (verified this run:
  itechguides, notesread, copyprogramming), and a keyboard GIPHY GIF is
  served from a library and never touches storage (wildandfreetools). So a
  GIF only watched in a chat was never a file, and the default run copies
  zero GIFs from it — stated as the condition in the TL;DR, the wall section,
  Method 1 steps 1 and 2, the readability section, FAQ Q1 and Q2, and "What
  to avoid". (3) THE SHARE TRAP — sharing a GIF out of the Gallery or a chat
  can flatten it to a still image: some share targets take only the first
  frame (verified this run: dev.to "Why Your GIF Turns Into a Still Image in
  Chats", which puts the blame on the format itself, a 1987 format storing
  every frame in full). The certain route copies the saved .gif file, never a
  re-shared copy — stated in the TL;DR, Method 1 step 3, FAQ Q3, and "What to
  avoid". (4) THE FILE IS SIMPLE — a GIF is an ordinary .gif file and the
  animation lives inside the file itself, no playback metadata, no sidecar,
  nothing like the slow-motion case; a byte-for-byte copy carries the whole
  animation. The check is playing one GIF back from the drive and watching it
  animate — stated in the TL;DR, the checking section, FAQ Q4, and "What to

  THREEMA READABILITY VERDICT (the critical question, verified from code at base 1de6c1b + live sources this run): (1) DEFAULT RUN COVERS GALLERY-SHOWING SAVED THREEMA PHOTOS — proven shape, with a stated condition. SnapDisk's default run queries the MediaStore images + videos tables only, with no folder filter (PhotoQuery.kt:23-36, the query call passes no selection at all); a Threema photo saved from a chat lands in the gallery as a "Threema" album — and the folder itself is proven by Threema's own open-source code, which writes saved images to Pictures/Threema and saved videos to Movies/Threema through the MediaStore, so the files arrive already indexed — and gallery apps read the media index, so a photo the gallery shows is a photo the default run sees. The album's existence in the gallery is the evidence the folder is indexed. This is the same shape as the WL-234 Viber, WL-236 Messenger, WL-238 Pinterest, and WL-239 Kik verdicts. The default run copies the WHOLE MediaStore library, not DCIM only (WL-207 correction, stated correctly throughout the article). (2) THE SAVE IS THE JOB — Threema is the one messaging app in the series where the save step is a switch that ships off. The auto-save switch, Settings, Media, Save media, carries defaultValue "false" in Threema's own open-source code (preference_media.xml), and Threema's own guides name it "Automatically Save Media" (First Steps) and "Auto-save to gallery" (app-configuration docs) — so the backup starts in the chat: turn the switch on for everything from now on, and save the backlog by hand. The manual save takes a list of selected messages (SaveMediaAsyncTask in Threema's own code), so long-press one photo, tap the others, and save the selection together — better than Kik's one tap per photo. Messages are deleted from Threema's servers immediately after delivery, so there is no server copy to recover from. (3) THE ONE-YEAR CLOCK — Threema deletes messages and media older than a year by default (Settings, Storage management — a tips guide states it plainly), so a photo left unsaved in an old chat is on a clock, not just in a queue; the article tells the reader to save the oldest chats first. (4) THE SAVE FOLDER IS EXACT, FROM THREEMA'S OWN CODE — not disputed between guides, but version-split: FileServiceImpl.copyMediaFileIntoPublicDirectory writes images to DIRECTORY_PICTURES plus "/Threema" and videos to DIRECTORY_MOVIES plus "/Threema" (MEDIA_PATH "Threema", app/build.gradle.kts:99); audio to Music/Threema, PDFs to Documents/Threema, other files to Downloads/Threema. On Android 9 and older the save went to /Threema/Threema Pictures and /Threema/Threema Videos at the top of internal storage. The generic guides name no path at all — only "the gallery" or "the phone folder" — so the article gives the check order — gallery first (Threema album), then Pictures/Threema, then Movies/Threema for videos, then the legacy folder on an old phone, plus Downloads/Threema for a photo sent as a file — in the TL;DR, the dedicated folder section, Method 1 step 3, Method 2, FAQ Q1, and "What to avoid". (5) THE DATA BACKUP FILE IS NOT A PHOTO BACKUP — the Threema-specific untangling: Threema's own FAQ says a data backup moves chats, groups, contacts, and ID to a new or reset phone and restores only on the same operating system, with media included only if "Include large media files" is on; Threema Safe holds ID, contacts, groups, and some settings only — no chats, no media. The file is one encrypted archive that opens only by restoring it into Threema, so a drive holding only that file holds no photos you can open; the file itself can be copied to USB as a file, as the second, encrypted copy. RESQ Toolbox, a free Windows app, backs up an Android phone's internal storage including the Threema backup over a USB cable to a PC, needing USB debugging on — named without endorsement, no USB leg from the phone.   .STATUSES READABILITY VERDICT (the critical question, verified from code at base fcf821b + live sources this run): (1) DEFAULT RUN CANNOT READ .STATUSES — proven. SnapDisk's default run queries the MediaStore images + videos tables only (PhotoQuery.kt:28-44); .Statuses is hidden from that index twice over — its name starts with a dot, which Android's media provider treats as hidden, and it contains a .nomedia file, which tells the media scanner to skip the folder and its subfolders (Android developer docs + AOSP MediaProvider behaviour, confirmed by live search this run; the .nomedia file inside .Statuses is visible in status-saver source code, which filters it out when listing the folder). So the one-tap whole-library backup copies zero statuses, silently. (2) DIRECT SAF PICK OF .STATUSES VIA SNAPDISK'S FROM PICKER: UNVERIFIED — stated as such in the article (TL;DR + Method 1 + "Can SnapDisk read .Statuses directly?" + FAQ Q2 + "What to avoid", WL-221–229 form). The picker is the generic system folder picker (MainActivity.kt:62, :71, OpenDocumentTree) opening with no folder pre-selected — no EXTRA_INITIAL_URI / initialUri anywhere in the code, no WhatsApp path handling anywhere in the app (0 matches for WhatsApp/.Statuses/.nomedia in the source) — and the system picker hides dot-folders. Status-saver apps prove the platform allows the access when an app builds the folder address directly (DocumentsContract.buildDocumentUri at .Statuses + takePersistableUriPermission + DocumentFile.listFiles); SnapDisk does not do that. Whether picking the parent Media folder and relying on SnapDisk's recursive walk (PhotoQuery.kt listTreeFiles/walkTree) to descend into .Statuses would work is likewise untested. (3) WHETHER THE CACHED FILE SURVIVES LONG ENOUGH TO COPY: UNVERIFIED — also stated as such; it is a cache, not a save, and no source guarantees how long it stays. THEREFORE Method 1 is the honest joined workflow, not a direct pick: view the status, copy the cached file out of .Statuses into a normal folder with a file manager (show hidden files on, copy not move), then point SnapDisk at that folder — or let the default run pick it up once the file sits in a normal folder. One code-grounded quirk carried in the article: a cached status file with no extension is skipped by SnapDisk's folder route, which only copies recognised photo/video extensions (PhotoQuery.kt isMediaName) — rename it with .jpg/.mp4 first.

THE .MOV VERDICT — re-verified this run from WL-216's chain (not re-read from AOSP this run; WL-216 read it directly): .mov → video/quicktime — INDEXED UNIVERSALLY. Directly read in the current AOSP upstream map: `video/quicktime qt mov` in external/mime-support/mime.types (main, line 1642) and mime.types-alt (main, line 4524); also in the Android 7.0 hardcoded table (libcore/net/MimeUtils.java, android-7.0.0_r36 tag: video/quicktime ← qt, mov, lines 748/750) and Android T MediaFile. The mechanism is ModernMediaScanner indexing a file into MediaStore Video iff its extension resolves via MimeTypeMap to a video/* MIME. developer.android.com supported-formats does NOT list .mov as a playable container — but that is decoding, not indexing; the scanner does not check codecs. ## WL-216 — Resolve the format-split contradiction in five articles: .mov and .dng indexed universally, .heic inconclusive (correction follow-up to WL-215, no new article)

- Owner: SEO/GEO lane lead. State: fix branch wl-216-format-split (commit 2b1d53a, pushed) and worklog-row branch wl-216-worklog (this branch, pushed) created by the lead from base 2dedc5fa; no PRs opened — the supervisor merges after readback.
  Evidence: base origin/main 2dedc5fa verified by readback after fetch (commit 2dedc5fa, "Merge pull request #402 from dzianisv/wl-215-worklog"); the local checkout was stale at 0de218e and was NOT trusted — fresh worktrees from origin/main. THE CONTRADICTION: WL-215 corrected the "What you give up" sentences in five articles to flat claims that the default run includes .mov/.heic/.dng because the query carries no format filter — but the SAME articles still carried "format split" hedges saying the opposite, that .mov/.heic/.dng indexing is device-dependent or "not promised the same way". Each article contradicted itself in print; this run makes the hedges agree with the verified truth. VERIFICATION (lead, this run, authoritative sources only — AOSP source and Android developer docs, every URL below read this run): MECHANISM — ModernMediaScanner (packages/providers/MediaProvider, AOSP main) indexes a file into MediaStore Images/Video iff its extension resolves via MimeTypeMap.getSingleton().getMimeTypeFromExtension() to an image/* or video/* MIME (MimeUtils.resolveMimeType → resolveMediaType; isImageMimeType/isVideoMimeType are prefix checks). MimeTypeMap delegates to MimeMap.getDefault(), built from upstream /etc/mime.types plus Android-specific overrides in android.mime.types (2019 cleanup CL d5e73ac: "takes the upstream /etc/mime.types as-is, and then layers on any Android-specific overrides... The 'android.mime.types' file in this CL is enough to keep all previous mappings intact, while also adding a handful of new popular MIME types such as HEIF"). .MOV → video/quicktime — INDEXED UNIVERSALLY. Directly read in the current AOSP upstream map: `video/quicktime qt mov` in external/mime-support/mime.types (main, line 1642) and mime.types-alt (main, line 4524); also in the Android 7.0 hardcoded table (libcore/net/MimeUtils.java, android-7.0.0_r36 tag: video/quicktime ← qt, mov, lines 748/750) and Android T MediaFile (Chromium's verbatim copy citing MediaFile.java). developer.android.com supported-formats does NOT list .mov as a playable container — but that is decoding, not indexing; the scanner does not check codecs. .HEIC — INCONCLUSIVE. Absent from both upstream mime.types files (zero matches for heif/heic/dng/adobe-dng in mime.types; mime.types-alt has `image/heic heic` L3846 and `image/heif heif` L3850, but no consumer of the -alt file was established — libcore's current main JavaLibrary.bp has NO mime.types references at all). Absent from the Android 7.0 table (no heif, no heic). Android T MediaFile maps only `heif` (image/x-heif), not `heic`. The 2019 CL says the override file adds HEIF, but android.mime.types itself could NOT be read directly: 404 on main and on the android-platform-14.0.0_r1 tag, and directory listings show it in neither libcore/net/ nor libcore/content/type/ on main. Supported-formats says HEIF decode is "Device optional. Check ImageDecoder.isMimeTypeSupported("image/heif")". Per the task rule the flat claim is softened to the hedged truth and this is stated here — nothing unverified is asserted. .DNG → image/x-adobe-dng — INDEXED UNIVERSALLY (preserved-mapping chain, stated transparently so the supervisor can audit it). `image/x-adobe-dng` ← `dng` in the Android 7.0 hardcoded table (line 554, a previous mapping); same in Android T MediaFile (Chromium verbatim copy); still present in current main MediaFile.java MTP block (FORMAT_DNG → image/x-adobe-dng, line 254). The 2019 CL states the override file keeps ALL previous mappings intact. Not in either upstream mime.types file — the verdict depends entirely on the Android override, which was not directly readable (see .heic). DEAD ENDS (do not repeat): cs.android.com search UI not fetchable; Gerrit PolyGerrit page needs JS (no content); libcore/net/MimeUtils.java on main 404 (file moved/deleted); android.mime.types 404 on main and 14.0 tag; no consumer found for the debian.mime.types.minimized(-alt) genrules; no caller of MimeMap.setDefaultSupplier found via web search. ## WL-215 — Correct the default-run scope in five articles: MediaStore, not DCIM or format (correction, no new article)

- Owner: SEO/GEO lane lead. State: fix branch wl-215-default-run (commit d1da2bb, pushed) and worklog-row branch wl-215-worklog (this branch, pushed) created by the lead from base 61df7c74; no PRs opened — the supervisor merges after readback.

THE DEFECT: five live articles carried the same wrong sentence in their "What you give up" paragraph — that SnapDisk's default run misses some photos ("if your photos live outside DCIM and the default run did not include them" / ".mov" / ".heic" / ".dng"). That is false. CODE RE-VERIFICATION (lead, this run, at base): PhotoQuery.kt:23-35 queryMediaStoreOldestFirst queries MediaStore.Images.Media.EXTERNAL_CONTENT_URI and MediaStore.Video.Media.EXTERNAL_CONTENT_URI, and queryMediaTable issues contentResolver.query(uri, projection, null, null, sortOrder) at :60 — selection null, so no folder filter and no MIME filter. BackupService.kt:634-641 enumeratePhotos confirms the routing: fromTreeUri != null goes to listTreeFiles (folder route), otherwise queryMediaStoreOldestFirst (default run). The .jpg/.heic/.dng/.mov extension lists are IMAGE_EXTENSIONS :130-133 and VIDEO_EXTENSIONS :134-137, used only by isMediaName :124-128, called only from walkTree :110 — the folder-walk route only. So the default run includes every photo/video MediaStore indexes, whatever its folder or format. .NOMEDIA VERIFICATION (lead, this run, web search): a folder containing an empty file named .nomedia is left out of the MediaStore index, so the default run never sees those photos — verified at dobr.app ("When the system finds a file named .nomedia in a folder, it leaves that folder out of the index"), pcnmobile.com ("Android defines .nomedia as the media-ignore filename. The media scanner ignores supported media in the directory containing that file"), and fileinfo.com ("It prevents apps like photo managers and video players from scanning and indexing the folder's contents"). That, plus files in app-private storage or files the scanner has not picked up yet, is what the manual Files-app route is actually the fallback for; no other fallback case is claimed in the fix.
  FIX (five articles, each in its own words, same sentence in the llms-full.txt passage for each): docs/321-backup-photos-to-usb.html:174 — folder location: the default run covers every photo MediaStore indexes, whatever folder it sits in, so a photo outside DCIM is included; the manual route is the fallback for photos MediaStore does not index (e.g. a .nomedia folder). docs/timelapse-videos-to-usb.html:170 and docs/slow-motion-videos-to-usb.html:170 — .mov: the default run reads the MediaStore Video table with no format filter, so a .mov clip is included like any .mp4; fallback is for clips MediaStore does not index. docs/motion-photos-to-usb.html:169 — .heic: the default run reads the MediaStore Images table with no format filter, so a .heic motion photo is included like any .jpg. docs/burst-photos-to-usb.html:169 — .dng: the default run reads the MediaStore Images table with no format filter, so a .dng burst frame is included like any .jpg. Also fixed the same wrong claim where it was quoted: docs/llms-full.txt passages at lines 2046 (motion), 2071 (burst), 2097 (slow-motion), 2151 (timelapse), 2179 (321) — same five sentences, line numbers unchanged; tool/growth/searches.md Query 167 (Facebook) row, two sentences — the behaviour note near :18944 ("Downloads and Pictures/Facebook are outside DCIM and are missed — so the Facebook route is the From-picker folder route, not the default run") and the brief near :18966 ("the default run covers DCIM/Facebook only because it walks DCIM recursively, that Downloads and Pictures/Facebook are missed by the default run") — both corrected to the MediaStore framing (default From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM are only the settings-screen labels until a folder is picked; with no folder picked the default run reads the whole library via MediaStore, PhotoQuery.kt:23-35, no folder filter and no MIME filter).   versions on the phone; Google Photos Storage saver
  compresses photos >16 MP to 16 MP and videos >1080p to
  1080p (per Google support). An exact file copy preserves
  capture dates/locations embedded in the originals. Three
  wipe checks before the old phone goes: photo count roughly
  matches, older photos and long videos open at full quality,
  drive copy opens. SnapDisk behaviour verified from the repo

  Key finding: a broken screen is three different problems.
  (1) Cracked screen, dead touch: OTG mouse enters your own
  PIN/pattern (a mouse never bypasses the lock); one port
  holds mouse or drive, not both — multi-port OTG hub, or
  Pro auto-backup on connect, solves it, but Pro only helps
  if set up before the break. (2) Black screen, phone on:
  video-out needs DisplayPort Alt Mode — DeX on Galaxy
  S8+/Note 8+/Z Fold/A90 5G only (Z Flip 5/6 output video,
  no DeX, per XDA); Pixel 8+ only (Pixel 6/7 hardware
  capable, Google left output off until Pixel 8); Motorola
  Ready For/Smart Connect, Huawei Easy Projection; OnePlus
  contested (12/13/Open per usbctohdmi vs 7+ flagships per
  salivity); Android 16 native desktop needs QPR3+ on Pixel
  8/9/10; an on-screen prompt can block video-out;
  DisplayLink dock is a reported (unverified) workaround.
  (3) Completely dead: no software route (Android Authority,
  verbatim); check Google Photos + microSD card first, then
  screen replacement or professional recovery. SnapDisk
  behaviour verified from the repo itself: minSdk 24
  (Android 7.0 floor), notification Backup tap, Pro $9.99
  auto-backup on connect, free 5 GB/run, FAT32 >4 GB files
  skipped and listed.

  replaceable 4400 mAh, 48 MP main + 5 MP front, 6-inch full

  "1 x USB 2.0 Type C OTG (support PD 3.0 charging)", micro SD

  P400M9 — Android 11.0, ARM A73 + A53, 4 GB/64 GB, 4-inch

  and autofocus, USB Port "1 x USB Type C OTG (support PD 2.0

  (desnoulez.fr/en/how-to-back-up-camera-photos-while-traveling-no-laptop-needed/
  — the same phone-as-bridge idea, copying a camera's card with
  the file manager. Generic, and a manual guide — and again about
  a camera's card); devicesfaq, "Frequently asked questions
  Panasonic Toughbook P-01K"
  (devicesfaq.com/en/frequently-asked-questions/panasonic-toughbook-p-01k
  — the only Toughbook-specific result: its backup answer is to
  connect the P-01K to a computer with a USB cable and copy the
  files with the file browser, or use Google Drive (15 GB free) or
  Google Photos. A FAQ page, not a guide — and the confirmation
  that the P-01K runs Android 8.1 with 16 GB of internal memory
  and a micro-USB charging port, with no USB-drive route offered at
  all); Photos to USB: OTG Backup
  (play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb
  — plug a pen drive into your phone, one tap copies every photo
  and video to the drive, no internet, no cloud, no account; free
  with ads, a one-time purchase removes the ads. The one-tap app
  alternative, generic Android, not a Toughbook guide);
  thegadgetians, "How to Transfer Files From Phone to USB Without

  (thegadgetians.com/how-to-transfer-files-from-phone-to-usb-without-computer/
  — connect a USB drive with an OTG adapter, open the file
  manager, select and copy files, then paste onto the USB drive.
  Generic Android, and a manual file-manager guide).
  Honest limits recorded in the article: the Toughbook line is
  mostly Windows laptops, so the article covers only the Android
  handhelds and tablets (FZ-N1, FZ-T1, FZ-S1, FZ-A3, FZ-L1,
  P-01K); the original FZ-N1 runs Android 6.0.1 (Panasonic Wiki),
  below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so it cannot run SnapDisk
  at all — only the FZ-N1 mk2, on Android 8.1 (Panasonic spec
  sheet), can; USB host support is listed only on the FZ-N1 mk2
  and the FZ-L1 (Panasonic's own spec sheets list their micro-USB
  port as "option to be host"), while host or OTG support is
  unconfirmed in the sources found on the FZ-T1 (Android 8.1,
  MobileGizmo), the FZ-S1 (Android 10, USB-C, Notebookcheck), the
  FZ-A3 (Android 9.0, USB-C, UL benchmarks), and the P-01K
  (Android 8.1, micro-USB, devicesfaq) — the drive mounting is the
  test on those models; the FZ-S1's microSD support is unconfirmed
  in the sources found, so the card is not leaned on for that
  model; most search results are about camera memory cards, with
  "Panasonic" meaning the camera brand, not the device — the
  article is about the photos stored on the Toughbook itself; the
  adapter differs by model (USB-C OTG on the FZ-S1/FZ-A3,
  micro-USB OTG on the FZ-N1 mk2/FZ-T1/FZ-L1/P-01K); Windows
  Toughbooks are out of scope entirely.

  data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you
  hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses
  photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop
  paying for storage. Neither route gives a folder of plain
  photo files on a USB drive.

  cashify lists "OTG Support, Yes" for the Toughphone and the
  Toughphone Max, the E10 review lists "USB-C 2.0 (OTG)", and
  JCB's own T10 page lists "USB-C with OTG support" — and
  every current model can run SnapDisk: the Toughphone runs
  Android 13, the Toughphone Max runs Android 12, the E10
  runs Android 15, the E50 runs Android 16, and the T10 tablet
  runs Android 16; on the E50 no source found mentions OTG at
  all, so the article tells owners of that model to plug a
  drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it
  instead of claiming OTG across the range. Two old JCB phones
  cannot run SnapDisk at all: the TP802 is a feature phone,
  not an Android phone, and the Toughphone Pro-Smart TP909
  from 2012 runs Android 2.3.5, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0
  minimum. The E10's specs are disputed between sources: one
  review's own spec table says Android 16 while its text and
  JCB's own site say Android 15, its chipset is a Helio G36
  per that review against an MT6765X per Clove and
  rugged.co.uk, and its RAM is 4 GB per that review against
  8 GB per rugged.co.uk — so the chipset and RAM are not leaned
  on in the article, and the Android version is taken as 15
  from JCB's own site. All current models have USB-C. All
  current models take a microSD card — up to 1 TB on the
  Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, and the E50, up to 512 GB on
  the E10, and up to 2 TB on the T10 tablet.
  JCB's own tools: the only JCB file advice found is the old
  TP802 manual's PC copy with a USB cable (Mass Storage); the
  stock photo backup is Google Photos, and the stock file
  manager is Files by Google; a microSD card is the local
  option on every current model; no JCB backup page points at
  a USB drive at all — none of them writes plain photo files
  to a USB drive automatically. Out of scope, named in the
  article: OTG support is unconfirmed on the E50, so owners of
  that model should check Settings > Storage before relying
  on it; the E10's specs are disputed between sources
  (Android 15/16, Helio G36 vs MT6765X, 4 GB vs 8 GB of RAM);
  the TP802 and the Toughphone Pro-Smart TP909 cannot run
  SnapDisk (feature phone / Android 2.3.5) — SnapDisk needs
  Android 7.0 or later.

  I found — the S10 Pro, the S20, the S30, the S30 Mini, the
  M6, the M8, and the T18 — and unconfirmed only on the S10,
  where PhoneMore lists microUSB 2.0 with no OTG mention, so
  the article tells owners of that model to check Settings >
  Storage before relying on it instead of claiming OTG across
  the range. Three models cannot run SnapDisk at all: the S10,
  the S20, and the S30 run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's
  Android 7.0 minimum, even though the S20 and the S30 list
  OTG support. The five models that can run SnapDisk all run
  Android 7.0: the S10 Pro, the S30 Mini, the M6, the M8, and
  the T18. The M8 is the only Nomu model I found with a USB-C
  port — every other model has microUSB 2.0. The specs are
  disputed between sources on several models: the S20 chipset
  (MediaTek MT6735 per Review Hub, MT6737T per UL benchmarks);
  the T18 chipset (MT6737 per gizmochina, MT6737T per
  unite4buy); the M8 Android version (7.0 per phonesdata and
  devicesfaq, 7.1 per unite4buy) and battery (2950 mAh per
  devicesfaq, 3000 mAh per unite4buy); the microSD size on the
  S10 Pro (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore, up to 32 GB per
  Smartprix), the S30 (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore, up to 32 GB
  per Notebookcheck), and the M6 (up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck,
  up to 64 GB per unite4buy). The S10 takes a microSD card up
  to 64 GB, the S30 Mini takes one up to 64 GB, and the T18
  takes one up to 32 GB — but a card is still not a USB drive:
  it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a
  card reader.
  Nomu's own tools: devicesfaq's backup advice for the S10 (a
  computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google
  Drive with 15 GB free and Google Photos in the cloud) points
  at a computer or the cloud, never at a USB drive, and the same
  template appears on the S30 Mini page; Google Photos (the
  stock photo backup on Nomu Android phones) backs photos up to
  Google's cloud; Google Drive (Android's default built-in
  service, 15 GB free) backs data up to Google's cloud; a
  microSD card (up to 64 GB on the S10, up to 64 GB on the S30
  Mini, up to 32 GB on the T18) is a real local copy, but the
  card stays in the phone and needs a reader elsewhere; a
  computer copy (connect the phone to a computer using the USB
  cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser)
  lands on the PC, not on a USB drive; no Nomu backup page
  points at a USB drive at all — none of them writes plain photo
  files to a USB drive automatically. Out of scope, named in the
  article: OTG support is unconfirmed on the S10, so owners of
  that model should check Settings > Storage before relying on
  it; the S10, the S20, and the S30 run Android 6.0, below
  SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so SnapDisk cannot run on
  them; the S20 chipset is disputed (MT6735 per Review Hub,
  MT6737T per UL benchmarks); the T18 chipset is disputed
  (MT6737 per gizmochina, MT6737T per unite4buy); the M8
  Android version is disputed (7.0 per phonesdata and
  devicesfaq, 7.1 per unite4buy) and its battery is disputed
  (2950 mAh per devicesfaq, 3000 mAh per unite4buy); the
  microSD size is disputed on the S10 Pro (64 GB per PhoneMore,
  32 GB per Smartprix), the S30 (64 GB per PhoneMore, 32 GB per
  Notebookcheck), and the M6 (32 GB per Notebookcheck, 64 GB
  per unite4buy); the M8 is the only Nomu model with USB-C, so
  owners of the microUSB models should buy a micro-USB OTG
  adapter, not a USB-C one — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or
  later.

  6.0, MediaTek MT6737M, 1 GB of RAM, 8 GB of storage, microSD

  (gadgets360.com/mobiles/news/energizer-hardcase-h240s-4g-feature-phone-1803739
  — "Avenir Telecom, a licensee of the Energizer brand, launched

  a 4G feature phone. Notably, the phone runs Android, but
  without access to Google Play - users will have to settle for
  the pre-installed apps on board." A launch report, not a guide
  — and the confirmation that the H240S runs Android 6.0 with no
  Google Play access); Energizer Ultimate U620S Pop, GSMArena
  (m.gsmarena.com/energizer_ultimate_u620s_pop-9548.php —
  "Cancelled … Android 9.0 … 128GB storage, microSDXC", "USB:
  USB Type-C 2.0, OTG". A spec table, not a guide — and the
  confirmation that the only Energizer phone I found with an OTG
  listing is a cancelled phone from the Ultimate line, not a Hard
  Case phone); Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing,
  com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb — the one-tap app alternative: copies
  the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new
  photos next time, warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit. Free with
  ads, one-time purchase to remove them. Generic Android, not an
  Energizer guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order,
  detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of
  every file); PhotoSaver Phone-to-Drive (Play listing,
  com.clevx.photosaver — a second one-tap app alternative: save
  photos and videos to any USB-C drive with one click, no cloud,
  no upload. Generic Android, not an Energizer guide, and it
  needs a USB-C connection, so it is no use on the microUSB Hard
  Case models); cloud routes — Google Photos syncs the gallery
  to Google's servers, Google Drive backs data up to Google's
  cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores data to a new
  phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google
  Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud
  backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage.
  Neither route gives a folder of plain photo files on a USB
  drive.
  Energizer specifics: OTG is unconfirmed across the whole Hard
  Case line — no Hard Case model lists USB OTG support in the
  sources I found; the spec tables list USB Type-C for the H550S,
  the H570S, the H590S, and the H620S and microUSB 2.0 for the
  H500S, with no OTG mention on any of them — so the article
  tells owners of every model to check Settings > Storage before
  relying on it instead of claiming OTG across the range; the
  only Energizer OTG listing found is the cancelled Ultimate
  U620S Pop, a different line that was never sold. Two models
  cannot run SnapDisk at all: the H280S and the H242S run KaiOS,
  not Android, and the H240S runs Android 6.0 with no Google Play
  access, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. The H550S runs
  Android 7.0, exactly the minimum; the H590S runs Android 8.0,
  the H620S runs Android 10, and the H621S runs Android 11; the
  H621S connector is unverified in the sources I found. The
  H570S specs are disputed between sources (Android 8.0, Helio

  per Gadgets360's 2018 launch story, against Android 9.0,
  MediaTek MT6739, 2 GB RAM, 16 GB storage, microSD up to 32 GB,

  H280S, and H242 pages; Google Photos (the stock photo backup on
  Energizer Hard Case Android phones) backs photos up to Google's
  cloud; Google Drive (Android's default built-in service, 15 GB
  free) backs data up to Google's cloud; a microSD card (up to
  32 GB on the H550S, up to 64 GB on the H500S, up to 32 GB on
  the H240S) is a real local copy, but the card stays in the
  phone and needs a reader elsewhere; a computer copy (connect
  the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of
  the files using the file browser) lands on the PC, not on a USB
  drive; no Energizer backup page points at a USB drive at all —
  none of them writes plain photo files to a USB drive
  automatically. Out of scope, named in the article: OTG host
  support is unconfirmed on every Hard Case model, so owners of
  every model should check Settings > Storage before relying on
  it; the H280S and the H242S run KaiOS, not Android, so SnapDisk
  cannot run on them; the H240S runs Android 6.0 with no Google
  Play access, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum; the H570S
  specs are disputed between sources (Android 8.0 / Helio P18 /
  3 GB / 32 GB / 4800 mAh per Gadgets360, against Android 9.0 /
  MT6739 / 2 GB / 16 GB / 6500 mAh per phonesdata and specspro);
  the H500S Android version is disputed (8.0 per pkgsm, 7.0 per
  mobilespecs and spec411); the H621S connector is unverified in
  the sources above, so owners of that model should check their
  own port before buying an adapter — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0
  or later.

  to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb —

  remove them. Generic Android, not a FOSSiBOT guide, and it does

  and Stop, or size verification of every file); cloud routes —
  Google Photos syncs the gallery to Google's servers, Google
  Drive backs data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and
  Google backup restores data to a new phone from Google's cloud,
  not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting
  compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day
  you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives a folder of
  plain photo files on a USB drive.
  FOSSiBOT specifics: OTG is confirmed on most of the line — the
  spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the F101, the F101 PRO,
  the F102, the F110 Pro 5G, and the F113, the F112 Pro's spec
  page lists USB OTG Type-C, and the F107 Pro's official-site
  spec says you can connect USB flash drives via an OTG cable —
  but the F101P's official page mentions OTG only as reverse
  charging and the F115 Ultra's spec data conflicts, so the
  article tells owners of those two models to check Settings >
  Storage before relying on it instead of claiming OTG across
  the range; all seven named models have USB-C, so a USB-C flash
  drive plugs straight in and a regular USB-A drive needs a
  USB-C OTG adapter; the F101 Pro takes a microSD card up to
  1 TB, and the F107 Pro and the F113 take one up to 2 TB — the
  F102's card size is the one disagreement in the sources, 1 TB
  per RottenWifi and 2 TB per Cashify — but a card is still not a
  USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else
  needs a card reader.
  FOSSiBOT's own tools: devicesfaq's backup advice for the F102
  (a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google
  Drive with 15 GB free and Google Photos in the cloud) points at
  a computer or the cloud, never at a USB drive; the F107 Pro
  manual's OTG mention is reverse charging only; Google Photos
  (the stock photo backup on FOSSiBOT Android phones) backs
  photos up to Google's cloud; Google Drive (Android's default
  built-in service, 15 GB free) backs data up to Google's cloud;
  a microSD card (up to 1 TB on the F101 Pro, up to 2 TB on the
  F107 Pro and the F113) is a real local copy, but the card stays
  in the phone and needs a reader elsewhere; a computer copy
  (connect the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a
  copy of the files using the file browser) lands on the PC, not
  on a USB drive; no FOSSiBOT backup page points at a USB drive
  at all — none of them writes plain photo files to a USB drive
  automatically. Out of scope, named in the article: the F101P's
  OTG host support is unlisted (official page mentions OTG only
  as reverse charging); the F115 Ultra's spec data conflicts
  (USB OTG listed as false while USB-C is also listed as false),
  so its OTG support is unverified; the original F101 went on
  sale in October 2020 and its Android version is unverified in
  the sources above, so owners of that model should check
  Settings > About phone — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later.

  phone and needs a reader elsewhere; a computer copy (connect
  the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy
  of the files using the file browser) lands on the PC, not on
  a USB drive; no Crosscall backup page points at a USB drive
  at all — none of them writes plain photo files to a USB drive
  automatically.

  file-manager guide); Dr.Fone, "4 Practical Ways to Transfer

  (drfone.wondershare.com/android-transfer/how-to-transfer-photos-from-android-to-usb.html
  — transfer photos with an OTG adapter, through Google Drive,

  Android to USB Drive (OTG, No Root)"
  (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb — connect the drive
  with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, and copy the files
  with a progress bar, with a FAT32 4 GB limit note. Generic
  Android, and a manual file-manager guide — the closest
  generic guide to this article's job, but it still needs you
  to pick the files yourself); YouTube, "How to Transfer
  Photos, Videos and any Files from Android Phone to USB
  Pendrive (USB Drive Tutorial)"
  (youtube.com/watch?v=ch1evyu5PPM — OTG adapter and the
  phone's built-in file manager, with a FAT32 or exFAT drive.
  Generic Android, and a manual file-manager guide);
  sekin.in, "How To Transfer Files From Android Phone To USB

  USB-OTG adapter and copy the files with Files by Google, or

  Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb — the one-tap

  them. Generic Android, not a IIIF150 guide, and it does not
  promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and
  Stop, or size verification of every file); cloud routes —
  Google Photos syncs the gallery to Google's servers, Google
  Drive backs data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and

  cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage
  saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops
  working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route

  backs data up to Google's cloud; Google Photos (the stock
  photo backup, "If what you want is to make a backup only of
  the photos and videos made with your IIIF150 you can use
  Google Photos") backs photos up to Google's cloud; a TF card
  (the FAQ pages' "Pass media files to memory card", shared
  SIM slot, up to 1 TB on the B3C, the Air3, and the B2 Ultra)
  is a real local copy, but the card stays in the phone and
  needs a reader elsewhere; the B3C user manual gives no

## WL-64 — Emulator end-to-end proof: full backup flow green (DONE)

- Owner: Product Lead agent. State: DONE Nov 18, 2026.
  Per Den's Nov 17 rule (product-framework commit 8803ffc):
  the emulator end-to-end pass is the proof; a real device is
  never required and never a gate; never ask him to test on
  his phone. Full backup flow verified on the emulator with
  virtual external storage, every step by evidence, not claims:
  disk detection (StorageReceiver mount broadcast -> offer
  notification) -> offer backup -> copy oldest-first (3 seeded
  photos, byte-verified at the destination) -> progress display
  (notification with progress bar, Pause/Stop actions) -> Pause
  (copy freezes, resume continues byte-exact) -> Stop (finished
  files kept, in-flight .part deleted) -> DONE notification
  ("Backup complete"). Evidence: emulator smoke run
  44219739812, green in 27m20s, JUnit XML in the run's
  smoke-evidence artifact: 18 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors,
  0 skipped — FullFlowInstrumentedTest (mount->offer,
  serviceCopies oldest-first + progress + DONE, pause/resume
  via notification actions, stop via notification action) plus
  NotificationScreenshotTest (offer/progress/done) and the
  engine/billing suites. PR #95 (14 commits), merge 57bc3ab,
  merged 2026-11-18T02:25:54Z; PR CI green.
  Two real findings fixed along the way, both in PR #95: (1) a
  genuine app bug — BackupService.publish() posted the terminal
  DONE/ERROR/LIMIT notification while still foreground, so
  stopForeground() removed it and the user never saw "Backup
  complete" (smoke runs 44199483316, 44203932318, 44210493197);
  fixed by detaching first (stopForeground(false)) and then
  posting via manager.notify(). (2) Two test-harness timing
  lessons, test-only: the DONE title must be asserted promptly
  at DONE time — the harness destroys MainActivity and removes
  both tasks ~15 s after DONE, which cancels the notification,
  so a poll after the ~17 s file verification always saw
  active=[] (run 44210493197's logcat proved the service DID
  post it: its sound played); and the seed DATE_TAKEN converge
  poll is now a warning, not a failure — the MediaStore scanner
  restores DATE_TAKEN from EXIF asynchronously, and with
  taken=0 the effective date (DATE_MODIFIED) still sorts
  sequentially seeded files oldest-first; the enumeration-order
  assert is the real gate.
  "Real-device proof (Pixel 9a + real USB disk)" removed from
  the Blocked (owner) lists in the v0.1.2 and v0.1.1 entries
  below (this row's PR). Honest limit: the emulator has no USB
  mount event, so the mount trigger itself is exercised via a
  synthetic broadcast, not a real OTG plug; the real-disk check
  (NTFS read-only detection) stays open in the Open section,
  route: Firebase Test Lab free tier, never his phone.

## WL-34 — Answer the Android 15 six-hour dataSync timeout before first release (DONE)

- Owner: Implementation lead. Due: Nov 19. State: DONE.
  Evidence: PR #30 (commit 12fe757, merge 81ed0e4); CI run
  43791513967 green (build pass, 1m47s).
  `BackupService.onTimeout` pauses with the same clean paused state
  as a disk detach (PAUSED + full error, `.part` kept, finished
  files kept), plain notification, then `stopSelf()`; `CopyControl.timedOut`
  unwinds the engine to `CopyResult.Paused` at the next buffer
  boundary; resume reuses the detach path (open the app first to
  reset the timer). A refused `startForeground` after the budget is
  exhausted surfaces as a full ERROR state, never a crash. Two unit
  tests prove the timeout path pauses cleanly and resumes byte-exact.
  Target-SDK note added to the implementation spec §2 (workspace spec
  mirror `docs/implementation-spec.md` — the repo carries no spec .md;
  the Notion hub page carries the same paragraph — verified present
  Nov 16, see the follow-up entry below). Timeout
  behavior verified against Android Developers "Foreground service
  timeouts". Real-device check closed by the Nov 17 emulator-proof
  rule (WL-64): the emulator end-to-end pass is the proof; never
  his phone.
